\chapter{Four Words for Following Directions}
\label{ch:la-avenida-y-seguir-recto}
\hlchaptermodality{401}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say la avenida, seguir, recto and cambiar, and use them to follow or change a route.}

Complete ES-C401-cambiar: follow an avenue, continue straight, and change route or transport.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[seguir]{seguir — follow what comes next}

\label{lesson:ES-C401-seguir}



\begin{quote}
Say train, flight, and beach. (\emph{El tren, el vuelo, la playa}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item ir — to go.
  \item continuar — another way to say to continue.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{se-GUIR}, two beats, weighted last. In \emph{gui}, the written \emph{u} is silent and keeps the \emph{g} hard: say \emph{geer}, not \emph{goo-eer}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{seguir} — \textquotedblleft{}to follow\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}to continue.\textquotedblright{}

It comes through Vulgar Latin \textbf{sequīre} from Latin \textbf{sequī}, \textquotedblleft{}to follow,\textquotedblright{} reshaped with the ending of \textbf{īre}, \textquotedblleft{}to go.\textquotedblright{} English \textbf{sequence} is a set in which one thing follows another; a \textbf{consequence} follows from a cause. Those words keep the same old motion.

In directions, \textbf{seguir} tells you to keep to the route:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{seguir la avenida} — follow the avenue;
  \item \textbf{seguir} — continue.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can tell someone to follow a named road or continue moving.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{seguir}
  \item \emph{seguir la avenida}
  \item \emph{seguir en tren}
  \item \emph{después del vuelo, seguir a la playa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \emph{follow the avenue}. (\emph{Seguir la avenida}.) What is the old idea shared with English \emph{sequence}? (\emph{One thing follows another}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cambiar]{cambiar — leave one route and take another}

\label{lesson:ES-C401-cambiar}



\begin{quote}
Name the flight, parking area, pass, and beach. (\emph{El vuelo, el aparcamiento, el abono, la playa}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el cambio — the related noun, a change or exchange.
  \item el destino — what may stay fixed when the route changes.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cam-BIAR}, two beats, weighted last. Keep \emph{mb} together as you move into the final \emph{iar}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{cambiar} — \textquotedblleft{}to change\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}to exchange.\textquotedblright{}

It comes from Latin \textbf{cambiāre}, which the Academy identifies as a word of Gaulish origin. Its exchange sense makes the core visible: leave one thing and take another. On a journey that may mean another train, route, or destination.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{cambiar de tren} — change trains;
  \item \textbf{cambiar de dirección} — change direction;
  \item \textbf{cambiar el destino} — change the destination.
\end{itemize}

English \textbf{change} reached its present form by a different Romance route, but it belongs to this same old family of exchange.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can follow an avenue, continue straight, and say when the journey changes.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cambiar}
  \item \emph{cambiar de tren}
  \item \emph{seguir recto por la avenida}
  \item \emph{con el abono, cambiar después del vuelo}
  \item \emph{cambiar la ruta del aparcamiento a la playa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the whole direction set: avenue, follow, straight, change. (\emph{La avenida, seguir, recto, cambiar}.) What older action sits inside \emph{cambiar}? (\emph{Exchanging one thing for another}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la avenida]{la avenida — the road by which you come}

\label{lesson:ES-C401-avenida}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the train}, \emph{the travel pass}, and \emph{the beach}. (\emph{El tren, el abono, la playa}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la calle — any street; an \emph{avenida} is usually broader.
  \item venir — to come, the idea that helps anchor this road.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-ve-NI-da}, four even vowels with the weight on \emph{ni}. The written \emph{v} has the same Spanish sound as \emph{b}; do not give it the English \emph{v}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la avenida} — \textquotedblleft{}the avenue,\textquotedblright{} usually a broad street.

The Academy derives \textbf{avenida} from Spanish \textbf{avenir}. The older noun could name something that came in force — especially a river's sudden rise — and also a road that leads, or lets people come, to a particular place. The modern broad city street grew from that road sense.

Keep the scale contrast:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{la calle} — the general word for a street;
  \item \textbf{la avenida} — usually a broad street, sometimes tree-lined.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name the broad street that begins a set of directions.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la avenida}
  \item \emph{la avenida y la calle}
  \item \emph{seguir y cambiar por la avenida}
  \item \emph{voy en tren a la avenida}
  \item \emph{tengo un abono y voy a la playa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word names a broad street, and which verb lies behind its history? (\emph{La avenida}; \emph{avenir}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[recto]{recto — keep the line straight}

\label{lesson:ES-C401-recto}



\begin{quote}
Name the beach and parking. (\emph{La playa, el aparcamiento}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item seguir — the action this direction modifies.
  \item derecha — right; a turn rather than a straight line.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{REC-to}, two beats, weighted first. The pair in the middle is \emph{k-t}.
  \item Keep \textbf{recto/resto} apart: \emph{REC-to} has \emph{k}; \emph{RES-to} has \emph{s}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{recto} — \textquotedblleft{}straight.\textquotedblright{}

It comes from Latin \textbf{rectus}, also \textquotedblleft{}straight.\textquotedblright{} English \textbf{rectilinear} keeps the straight-line meaning, and every \textbf{rectangle} is built from straight sides and right angles.

For a route, put it after the action:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{seguir recto} — continue straight.
\end{itemize}

Do not let the exam's near-neighbour replace it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{recto} — straight;
  \item \textbf{resto} — the rest, the remainder.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can combine an action and a quality into the direction \emph{seguir recto}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{recto}
  \item \emph{recto, resto}
  \item \emph{seguir recto por la avenida}
  \item \emph{cambiar y después seguir recto}
  \item \emph{seguir recto al aparcamiento y después a la playa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \emph{continue straight}. (\emph{Seguir recto}.) Which consonant keeps \emph{recto} apart from \emph{resto}? (\emph{K rather than s}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{route recall one — hear the chain, then rebuild it}

\label{lesson:ES-C401-route-recall-1}



\begin{quote}
Give the four-word chain from a broad road to a changed route. (\emph{La avenida, seguir, recto, cambiar}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You are on \textbf{la avenida}. The instruction is \textbf{seguir recto}. Then the route changes: \textbf{cambiar de dirección}. Say those three steps again without the English prompts.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la avenida}
  \item \emph{seguir recto}
  \item \emph{cambiar de dirección}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say the route in one line. (\emph{Seguir recto por la avenida y después cambiar de dirección}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{route recall two — rebuild it from the change}

\label{lesson:ES-C401-route-recall-2}



\begin{quote}
Start with \emph{change}, then say \emph{avenue}, \emph{follow}, and \emph{straight}. (\emph{Cambiar, la avenida, seguir, recto}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Someone says \textbf{cambiar}. Ask which road: \textbf{¿Qué avenida?} Then recover the instruction \textbf{seguir recto}. The same four words now survive a different cue.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cambiar}
  \item \emph{¿Qué avenida?}
  \item \emph{seguir recto}
  \item \emph{cambiar y seguir recto por la avenida}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Without looking back, name and use all four direction words. (\emph{La avenida; seguir recto; cambiar de dirección}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
